clue.text: Compiled offers seen in cards date hands out

parts.note: a pack is a full deck of playing cards
an age is a period or era, as is a date in the sense of a time
deals means distributes, as a dealer does with cards

explanation.surface: A card game: someone dealing out hands while a date is noted, with offers floating about.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-table picture (cards, hands, deals) hides three plain synonyms laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Bundled sales offers, several items sold together for one price, are what this phrase names.

clue.text: Cut by this person good plait is botched — as this

definitions.text: Cut by this person good plait is botched — as this

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are split open by the single letter for the setter
a botched job is messed up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the setter speaking of themself, giving I

explanation.surface: A hairdresser confesses a plait went wrong when they cut it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is botched' scrambles G and PLAIT; 'Cut by' puts I inside. The whole clue also describes the result: a plait, done badly, looks like this.
explanation.definitionFit: A single braid of hair hanging at the back of the head is the hairstyle meant.

clue.text: Hack meets the French outsiders in Romandy — it's usual to dine with them

definitions.text: it's usual to dine with them

parts.note: to hack is to cut roughly
le is French for 'the'

indicators.note: the outer letters of the word that follows are taken, the pair at either end

explanation.surface: A hack journalist meets French people in Romandy, the French-speaking part of Switzerland, where dining is customary.
explanation.walkthrough: Romandy is French-speaking Switzerland, which makes 'the French' read as people rather than LE.
explanation.definitionFit: Knives, forks and spoons are the utensils people normally eat their meals with.

clue.text: Nearly all clap ape surprisingly singing like this?

indicators.note: the letters end up in a surprising new order
nearly the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: An ape clapping along to music, which would indeed surprise most onlookers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' trims ALL to AL; 'surprisingly' shuffles AL, CLAP and APE together.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian phrase describes voices performing without instrumental accompaniment, the singers alone.

clue.text: Turn out object, getting promoted

parts.note: an end is an aim or object, as in 'to that end'
up as in moved up, raised to a higher level

explanation.surface: An objection turns out well and someone gets promoted.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean to finish in a certain state or to prove eventually to be so.

clue.text: Leader of rising theatre in European city

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters are read from bottom to top
the theatre word is placed inside the city

parts.note: Rome is the Italian capital
rep is short for repertory theatre

explanation.surface: The head of a theatre company on the up in some European city.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rising' reverses the whole assembly, giving ROREPME before the turn; 'Leader' is a ruler, not the first letter of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch ruling an empire is a supreme ruler, the head of a state.

clue.text: One watches Waterloo KO Uttoxeter, missing part of it

indicators.note: parts of the opening and closing words are left off, so the answer sits inside the phrase

explanation.surface: A spectator sees Waterloo knock out Uttoxeter, a Staffordshire market town, in some sporting contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing part of it' drops WATER from the front and TOXETER from the end, leaving the run hidden in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry or watchman is posted specifically to keep watch.

clue.text: One gives inside info of Cockney three-piece on phone

parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang 'whistle and flute' means suit, shortened to its first word; a three-piece is a suit
the blower is old British slang for the telephone

explanation.surface: A Cockney in a three-piece suit passes on secrets by telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang drops the rhyming word: 'whistle and flute' for suit becomes just 'whistle'. 'on' simply joins the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: An informant who exposes wrongdoing inside an organisation is what this term describes.

clue.text: Say, Fagin and Artful appearing in not so successful musical

indicators.note: the two words describing Dickens's characters are placed within the comparison word

parts.note: less means to a smaller degree, not so much
Fagin, the grasping old fence in Oliver Twist, is an example of a miser, 'Say' marking an example
artful means skilful or able, also the Artful Dodger's nickname

explanation.surface: Characters from Oliver Twist appear in a stage show that did not do so well.
explanation.walkthrough: Fagin and the Artful Dodger point to the musical Oliver!, a red herring; 'Say' marks Fagin as an example, and 'successful' belongs to the definition, not to 'not so'.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running stage musical based on Victor Hugo's novel is one of the West End's biggest hits.

clue.text: Traditional institution that's taken in the PM

definitions.text: Traditional institution that's taken in the PM

parts.words: Traditional institution that's taken in the PM
parts.note: PM looks like the Prime Minister, but here it is post meridiem, the afternoon, when a traditional British meal is taken

explanation.surface: A long-standing tradition accepted by the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'the PM' as the Prime Minister; it is the afternoon. 'Taken' is eaten or drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: An afternoon meal of tea, sandwiches and cakes is a cherished British custom.

clue.text: Condemn daughter and Romeo getting admission to elope at sea

indicators.note: the letter is let into the middle of the jumbled word
at sea means confused, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A father condemns his daughter and her Romeo for eloping on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' shuffles ELOPE to EPLOE; 'getting admission to' puts R inside it, after D.
explanation.definitionFit: To condemn something is to disapprove of it strongly and express regret.

clue.text: Seen in drink, swimmer in distress

indicators.note: the fish is found inside the drink word

parts.note: to sup is to drink
a hake is a fish, a swimmer

explanation.surface: A fish spotted in someone's drink, causing them distress.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsettle or upset someone badly is to rattle them, a phrasal verb meaning distress.

clue.text: Present for each group of students …

parts.note: per means for each, as in 'per head'
a form is a class or year group in a British school

explanation.surface: A gift for each class at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a noun, a gift; it is the verb, to put on a show.
explanation.definitionFit: To present a play or act is to put it on before an audience.

clue.text: … some students possessing nothing, with yen to make cash

indicators.note: the learners hold the zero between them

parts.note: L is a learner, as on a British L-plate; several learners give a run of them
O is zero, nothing
Y is the abbreviation for the yen, the Japanese currency

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: broke students borrowing yen to raise money.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 12 Across but adds nothing to the parse. 'possessing' puts O among three Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: It is British slang for money, as in 'raking in the readies'.

clue.text: Speech from minister before one goes to the dispatch box?

definitions.text: Speech from minister before one goes to the dispatch box?

parts.words: Speech from minister before one goes to the dispatch box?
parts.note: the dispatch box suggests a government minister addressing Parliament, but the minister is a clergyman and the box a coffin for one who has been dispatched

explanation.surface: A government minister's speech before stepping up to the Commons despatch box.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dispatch Box is where ministers speak in the House of Commons; here the minister is a priest and the box a coffin.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest gives these religious ceremonies to someone who is about to die.

clue.text: Small sides in vessel

parts.note: teams are sides in a game
hip means fashionable, in

explanation.surface: Small teams in a boat, perhaps rowing crews.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word placing sides inside the vessel; it is a synonym, HIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship driven by steam power is a kind of seagoing vessel.

clue.text: Actors' private parts

parts.note: the phrase hints at something rude, but means the areas of a theatre out of public view, where actors prepare

explanation.surface: A cheeky reference to performers' genitals.
explanation.walkthrough: The innuendo is the joke: the 'private parts' are dressing rooms and wings, not anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: The dressing rooms and wings behind a theatre's stage are off limits to the audience.

clue.text: Regularly avoided coast's air or she would get kind of cold

indicators.note: every second letter is skipped, so the 1st, 3rd, 5th and so on are kept

explanation.surface: She would catch a cold if she didn't steer clear of sea air on the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly avoided' discards the even letters of COASTSAIRORSHE, keeping the odd ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflammation of the nose and throat with heavy mucus is the condition that comes with a head cold.

clue.text: Bird's down

definitions.meaning: to down a drink is to gulp it

explanation.surface: A bird is feeling low, or a bird's soft feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking the two definitions; it is not a possessive and 'down' is not feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a migrating songbird and a verb for gulping food or drink.

clue.text: Part of building left to enter flipping opposite part of building!

indicators.note: the letter for left goes inside the other part
flipping means turning over, so the word is reversed

parts.note: the roof is at the opposite end of a building from the lowest level

explanation.surface: An exasperated builder's remark: 'Part of the building's gone flipping wrong!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' reads like a mild British swearword; it reverses ROOF to FOOR, and 'to enter' puts L inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The ground surface or a storey of a building, which you walk on.

clue.text: Delicacy that's unlimited if in Essex

indicators.note: the phrase loses its outer limits, its first and last letters, leaving the run within

explanation.surface: A fine food that is plentiful in the county of Essex, east of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicacy' suggests a food; here it is subtlety. 'unlimited' strips the I and X from the ends of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicacy can mean refined skill or tact in handling something, which is subtlety.

clue.text: Beautiful things Tolkien characters must carry concealed

indicators.note: the creatures hold the other word inside them

parts.note: orcs are the brutish creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth
hid means concealed

explanation.surface: Tolkien's characters secretly carrying some treasure, as in The Lord of the Rings.
explanation.definitionFit: Exotic flowers prized for their beauty are an example of beautiful things.

clue.text: Survive old pirate's sword with edges eroded by time

indicators.note: the sword word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: a cutlass is the short curved sword of pirate stories

explanation.surface: An old pirate's blade, its edges blunted over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with edges eroded' trims CUTLASS to UTLAS; 'by' just joins it to T.
explanation.definitionFit: To survive someone or something is to live or last longer than them.

clue.text: Strained, pickled, sealed

definitions.meaning: closed so nothing gets in, as with an airtight lid

explanation.definitionFit: The one word means taut, drunk and closely sealed, three separate senses.

clue.text: Manic crashes involving one second-class vehicle

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take in the numeral
the letters crash and come out in a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
B is a second-class grade, after A

explanation.surface: A manic driver crashes into a second-rate car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crashes' shuffles MANIC; 'involving' puts I in, giving MINICA before B.
explanation.definitionFit: A small taxi that must be booked in advance, rather than hailed, is a type of vehicle.

clue.text: What stops listener or two keeping quiet?

definitions.text: What stops listener or two keeping quiet?

indicators.note: the pair of hearing words hold the musical letter between them

parts.note: two words for a listener: ear, and lug, British slang for an ear
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A riddle: what keeps a listener, or two, in silence?
explanation.walkthrough: Lug is British slang for an ear, so 'listener or two' gives two words for one organ. The whole clue also defines the answer: it blocks a listener and keeps things quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft plug pushed into the ear canal blocks out sound.

clue.text: Man maybe missing son after joining army, so warlike

indicators.note: the island piece comes after the army word, joined on

parts.note: a host is a multitude, an archaic word for an army

indicators.note: the letter for son is left out

parts.note: the Isle of Man is an island, so Man is an example of an isle

explanation.surface: A man joins the army after losing his son, which makes him aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital M hides the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea; 'maybe' marks it as an example. Host is an old word for an army.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfriendly and aggressive, opposed as an enemy would be, is to be warlike.

clue.text: Display with seals clapping should follow these

parts.note: a show is a display
stoppers seal bottles

explanation.surface: A seal show at the zoo, the animals clapping their flippers at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seals clapping' paints performing animals; seals are bottle stoppers and the clapping belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Performances so good that the audience applauds long enough to halt the show.
